title: When the Bell Wakes
premise: Folklorist Orsen Hartwell arrives in the fog-bound village of Bellwether to record its songs, but the villagers refuse to sing any verse twice, and every door in the parish is counted each night. When Orsen's sleep recordings capture a second voice answering questions no one asked aloud, they discover the village has been keeping something fed with half-sung hymns for two hundred years — and their arrival has interrupted the feeding. Trapped through one long night as the bell tolls the hours and the thing wearing familiar voices comes calling, Orsen must choose between the loyalty of the villagers who shelter them and the truth that the invitation was never meant to end. At dawn, Orsen sings the forbidden verse whole, breaking the pact: the bell falls silent forever, but Orsen leaves knowing they were invited in all along.
about_author: Ivo Hartwell is the pen name of a former archivist who spent years cataloguing oral histories in coastal parishes before turning to fiction. They write horror rooted in folk custom, drawn to stories where politeness is the first casualty.

chapters.title: The Counting of Doors
chapters.summary: Orsen arrives in Bellwether at dusk, welcomed warmly by innkeeper Maren Cole, who locks the inn's doors at exactly nine and counts them aloud. POV: Orsen. The emotional beat is uneasy charm — hospitality with rules attached, and a village that goes quiet whenever Orsen mentions recording songs.

chapters.title: Half a Hymn
chapters.summary: Orsen records old Tam Yew singing a harvest hymn; he stops mid-verse, pale, refusing to sing it twice even when paid. Maren confiscates nothing but warns him gently about 'finishing things.' POV: Orsen. The beat is curiosity curdling into unease as three villagers independently beg him not to play the tape back.

chapters.title: What Answers in Sleep
chapters.summary: Reviewing overnight room recordings, Orsen hears themselves talking in sleep — and a second voice, dry and patient, answering questions Orsen never asked. It knows their name, their mother's lullaby, the reason they really came. POV: Orsen. The beat is dread: the recorder has caught something that was already listening.

chapters.title: The Bell That Tolls Early
chapters.summary: The church bell rings at midnight though the tower has been sealed for decades. Villagers light candles in windows and stand in doorways counting. Maren admits the village 'keeps an appointment' and begs Orsen to leave before the next full dark. POV: Orsen. The beat is the first open crack in the village's polite facade.

chapters.title: Voices Wearing Neighbors
chapters.summary: Tam Yew knocks at 2 a.m., speaking in a voice too smooth, asking to be let in 'to finish the song.' Orsen refuses; by morning Tam remembers nothing and weeps. POV: Orsen, with a brief interlude from Maren's journal. The beat is grief — the thing uses love as a key.

chapters.title: The Ledger of Invitations
chapters.summary: In the church vestry, Orsen finds a ledger listing every outsider welcomed since 1798, each entry closed with a date of departure — except the newest page, already bearing Orsen's name, undated. POV: Orsen. The beat is cold revelation: Orsen wasn't a guest; they were an expected delivery.

chapters.title: Loyalty's Price
chapters.summary: Maren confesses the pact: the village feeds the bell-thing half-songs so it never asks for whole ones, and outsiders who hear too much must either join the count or be given. She offers Orsen a place among them. POV: Orsen. The beat is the thematic crux — belonging offered at the cost of truth.

chapters.title: The Longest Hour
chapters.summary: The bell begins tolling without pause. Doors rattle, candles gutter, and voices of Orsen's dead mother call from the well. The villagers hold hands in the square, singing the half-hymn over and over, fraying. POV: Orsen amid the crowd. The beat is siege terror and communal desperation.

chapters.title: The Whole Verse
chapters.summary: As the last candle dies, Orsen understands: the thing cannot bear completion. Standing in the square, they sing the harvest hymn entire, alone, voice cracking, while the second voice screams through every window. POV: Orsen. The beat is defiant climax — truth chosen over safety, identity claimed rather than granted.

chapters.title: Silence at Sunrise
chapters.summary: Dawn comes to a village without a bell and without its pact; some villagers weep with relief, others with loss of the belonging they'd sold. Orsen records one final track — their own voice, sung once, never twice — and walks out past the uncounted doors. POV: Orsen. The beat is bittersweet resolution: free, changed, and no longer sure which side of the invitation they stood on.
